content: The periodic table of chemical elements is a structured, tabular representation of all known chemical elements. Its creation is widely attributed to Dmitri Mendeleev, a Russian chemist, in 1869. Mendeleev designed the table to highlight recurring trends, or periodic patterns, in the properties of elements. Over time, the table has been refined and expanded as new elements were discovered and as theoretical models of chemical behavior evolved. Today, the periodic table is an essential tool in chemistry, providing a systematic framework for classifying and comparing the chemical properties of elements. It is also widely used in physics, biology, engineering, and industry. The modern periodic table contains 117 confirmed elements as of January 27, 2008, with element 118 synthesized but not yet confirmed at that time. The table is organized in rows (periods) and columns (groups) to reflect periodic trends in chemical properties. Elements in the same group share similar properties due to their valence electron configurations, while elements in the same period correspond to the filling of a quantum electron shell. The periodic table has various display formats. The standard table is the most common, but alternative versions exist, such as vertical scrolling tables for narrow pages, detailed tables with atomic masses, and tables highlighting specific properties like electronegativity or electron configurations. Some versions integrate the f-block elements (lanthanides and actinides) inline with the main table, while others shade blocks or valences to emphasize trends. The arrangement of the periodic table demonstrates periodic chemical properties, such as atomic number (the number of protons in the nucleus). Rows are arranged so that elements with similar properties fall into the same vertical columns, or groups. According to quantum mechanical theories, each horizontal row, or period, corresponds to the filling of a quantum electron shell. The table is divided into s-, p-, d-, and f-blocks based on electron configurations. In printed tables, each element is typically listed with its symbol and atomic number. Many versions also include additional information, such as atomic mass, abbreviated electron configuration, electronegativity, and common valence numbers. As of 2006, the table includes 117 confirmed elements, 92 of which occur naturally on Earth, while the rest are synthetic and produced in particle accelerators. Elements 43 (technetium) and 61 (promethium) are synthetic despite having lower atomic numbers than uranium (92). Elements 93 (neptunium) and 94 (plutonium) are synthetic but have been found in trace amounts on Earth. The periodic table's primary value lies in its ability to predict the chemical properties of elements based on their position. Properties vary differently when moving vertically along groups compared to horizontally along periods. Groups are vertical columns in the table and are considered the most important classification method. For example, alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, halogens, and noble gases are well-defined groups. Some groups, like Groups 14 and 15, display fewer similarities and are referred to by their group numbers. Periods are horizontal rows in the table. While groups are the most common way to classify elements, some regions of the table exhibit significant horizontal trends, such as in the d-block (transition metals) and f-block (lanthanides and actinides). These blocks often form substantial horizontal series of elements. Modern quantum mechanical theories explain group trends by proposing that elements within the same group have similar valence electron configurations, which account for their similar properties. Elements in the same group also show patterns in atomic radius, ionization energy, and electronegativity. From top to bottom in a group, atomic radii increase due to more filled energy levels, making electrons farther from the nucleus. Ionization energy decreases because it becomes easier to remove an electron, and electronegativity decreases due to the increasing distance between valence electrons and the nucleus. In periods, elements show trends in atomic radius, ionization energy, electron affinity, and electronegativity. Moving left to right across a period, atomic radius decreases as additional protons and electrons pull the electrons closer to the nucleus. This decrease in atomic radius causes ionization energy to increase, as more energy is required to remove an electron. Electronegativity also increases due to the stronger pull exerted by the nucleus on electrons. Electron affinity shows a slight trend, with metals generally having lower electron affinity than nonmetals, except for noble gases. Noble gases (Group 18) have full valence shells, making them highly stable and unreactive. Helium is the most inert element, while reactivity slightly increases with heavier noble gases due to their larger electron shells. However, their reactivity remains very low overall. Halogens (Group 17) are one electron short of a full valence shell, making them highly electronegative and reactive. Fluorine is the most electronegative element, and electronegativity decreases with increasing period. Halogens form acids with hydrogen, such as hydrofluoric acid (HF) and hydrochloric acid (HCl). The acidity of these acids increases with higher periods due to the stability of larger ions like iodide (I-) compared to smaller ions like fluoride (F-). Transition metals (Groups 3 to 12) exhibit both horizontal and vertical trends. Their reactions often involve coordinated species, and differences between adjacent groups are usually not dramatic. Lanthanides (elements 57–71) and actinides (elements 89–103) have even more similar chemical properties, making their separation challenging, which is important in nuclear power applications. The structure of the periodic table is determined by electron configurations, particularly valence electrons. Elements with the same number of valence electrons are grouped together. The type of orbital in which the outermost electrons reside determines the element's block (s-, p-, d-, or f-block). The number of valence electrons determines the group, while the total number of electron shells determines the period. As atomic number increases, outer-shell electrons occupy orbitals with higher energy and average distance from the nucleus. Historically, the periodic table evolved from early attempts to classify elements. In ancient Greece, Aristotle proposed four elements: air, fire, earth, and water. This idea was later dismissed as real chemical elements were discovered. Johann Wolfgang Döbereiner identified triads of similar elements in 1829, proposing the Law of Triads, where the middle element's atomic weight was the average of the other two. John Newlands proposed the Law of Octaves in 1865, noting that elements with similar properties recurred at intervals of eight. However, his law failed for elements with higher atomic masses and could not accommodate noble gases. Dmitri Mendeleev is credited with creating the first periodic table in 1869. He arranged elements by atomic mass but made adjustments to better align with their properties. Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties, which were later confirmed. His work was validated by the discovery of electronic structures in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Modern periodic tables reflect our understanding of electron configurations, grouping elements into s-, p-, d-, and f-blocks. Glenn T. Seaborg's identification of transuranic elements further refined the table, integrating lanthanides and actinides.
